pronunciation.approximation: SHOH-lotl, long ō on both syllables.
pronunciation.note: Xōlōtl carries two long ō vowels, both preserved in the restoration; the final -tl is Nahuatl's signature consonant cluster, released laterally — the sound every visitor learns on the name of the axolotl, the water-monster that shares his name and, in myth, his skin.

domains.title: The Twin in the Dark
domains.subtitle: Venus's Evening Star, the Dog-Guide, and the Last Transformation
domains.lead: Xōlōtl is the twin who goes down with the sun: brother of Quetzalcōātl, guide of the dead across the underworld's river, and the god who turned himself into maize, maguey, and finally the axolotl rather than be sacrificed. He is the Aztec soul's ferryman — and the lake that still bears his name.

cards.name: The Dog
cards.desc: His animal: the guide that leads the dead across the ninefold river of Mictlān.

cards.name: The Evening Star
cards.desc: Venus at dusk — his station, twin to his brother's morning star.

cards.name: The Axolotl
cards.desc: His final disguise: the water-monster of Xochimilco, gilled and smiling, that shares his name.

cards.name: The Empty Sockets
cards.desc: The codices show him weeping his eyes out at the gods' sacrifice — grief itself, dog-eared.

mythology.lead: Xōlōtl's myths run on twoness: twin of the morning star, guide of the dying sun, the god who is always the second of a pair — and always the one who goes down into the dark.

myths.title: Across the Nine Waters
myths.text: The Aztec dead journeyed four years through Mictlān's nine levels, and at the deep river it was the dog — Xōlōtl's creature — who swam them across: a soul whose family had mistreated dogs in life found no ferryman, while one buried with his red dog had a guide already in the grave (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, trans. Anderson & Dibble — the funeral rites of the dead's journey). The funeral rite killed a dog 'the color of fire' and laid it with the dead to carry its master home. Among the world's psychopomps, he is the only one who comes as a pet — the escort you raised from a pup, not a paid professional of the crossing, and the myth's quiet claim is that loyalty outlasts the life that earned it.

myths.title: The God Who Hid
myths.text: At the creation of the fifth sun the gods gathered at Teotihuacan to sacrifice themselves and set the new sun moving (Leyenda de los Soles, Codex Chimalpopoca). Xōlōtl refused to die: he fled, weeping so hard his eyes fell from their sockets, and hid — as the twin-stalked maize, as the doubled maguey, and at last as the axolotl in the lake. They found him even there, and he died like the rest. The myth is the Aztec anatomy of the price of survival — and of the god who begged to live and serves death anyway: the one who ran is precisely the one the dead meet at the river, as if the underworld drafted its guide from the only god who had tried, with everything he had, to stay on this side of it.

myths.title: Venus Split in Two
myths.text: Quetzalcōātl is Venus as morning star, herald of the light; Xōlōtl is Venus as evening star, which follows the sun into darkness (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 7 — the star cycles and the binding of the years). The astronomy is exact — one planet, two appearances — and the myth makes it biography: one twin leads the dawn out of the night, the other escorts the day into it. Together they keep the star's whole circuit, and the world's whole hope: nothing in the Aztec sky set unaccompanied, and no light went down into the dark without the god of guides riding it.

myths.title: The Bones of the Fathers
myths.text: When the fifth age needed people, Quetzalcōātl descended to Mictlān for the bones of the dead, and the later tellings send Xōlōtl with him as the one who knows the road — past Mictlāntēcutli's traps to the underworld council, where the lord of the dead set impossible conditions: sound my conch, which no breath will blow, and circle my realm four times without setting the burden down (Leyenda de los Soles; cf. the Histoyre du Mechique). The bones, ground in a bowl and sprinkled with the gods' own blood, became humankind — every Aztec child made of the dead, carried up past the watchful lord by knowledge of the road back. That the tellings choose the dog-brother for the escort is the myth's own logic: who better to know Mictlān's way than the god who ferries it daily?

lore.syncretism: The friars identified him with the devil's lesser angels, but the people kept him closer to a saint of the road: the dog that guards the grave and guides the traveller survived in Mexican folk custom, and the hairless xoloitzcuintli — the national dog, named from his name — was never exorcised. Scholars pair him with every underworld canine from Cerberus to Anubis, and the Maya twins' underworld journey in the Popol Vuh runs on his same road. The axolotl, his water-form, became Mexico's ambassador-species: the smiling face of conservation itself.
lore.culturalLegacy: The axolotl — Ambystoma mexicanum, the salamander that never grows up, regenerating limbs and heart — took his name into every biology classroom on earth; its survival in Xochimilco's canals is now a national project. The xoloitzcuintli dog is Mexico's national breed, and Dante's Divine Comedy has, in the Mexican imagination, a local answer: the Xolo that carries you across. Frida Kahlo painted her xolos; the 2018 animated films gave him to the world's children.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Xōlōtl is the god of the way through. He did not want the job — he wept, hid, and transformed to escape it — and he does it still: the sun into the dark, the dead across the river, the lost back home. He asks the guide's question, which is also the mourner's: who walks with you into the night — and whom, in your turn, will you guide?

The axolotl's refusal to grow up — keeping its gills, its larval smile, its power to regrow a heart — has made it the scientist's darling and the city's emblem, and it is the god's final joke: the deity who begged not to die survives as the animal that regenerates everything. Xōlōtl's question is the guide's own: transformation is not escape — but sometimes, in the last lake, it is enough.

lore.archaeology: Colima's ceramic dogs — plump, tumored, dancing, two thousand years old — are the west-Mexican ancestors of his cult, buried in shaft tombs to guide their masters. Aztec dog-effigy vessels and the Florentine Codex's account of the funeral dog detail the central-Mexican rite. Xochimilco's chinampa system — the floating gardens where the last wild axolotls hold on — is a UNESCO World Heritage site, the god's water-form's last stronghold, guarded by canals older than the Aztec state.
lore.originalScriptNote: The codices write him as what he is: the dog-headed god, often shown twisted in transformation — half into maize, half into the water-beast — with the twin's ball-court and the Venus star in his glyphic entourage. The name and the animal (xōlōtl, "water monster," the axolotl) are one word: the god hiding inside his own spelling.
